slides.title: When2Ask: clarification timing
slides.script: Large language models make it easy to build agents that follow new instructions without task-specific training. But stronger reasoning cannot recover a user preference that was never given. A robot may guess the wrong object, or interrupt the user when useful work is already possible. We study when it should ask. There is also a systems cost: repeatedly asking a generative model to make a small ASK-or-CONTINUE decision adds API latency and expense. Our question is whether a specialized judgment model can preserve the reliability of clarification with less decision overhead. Our main contribution is a controlled robotic benchmark to test that trade-off, rather than assuming one model will win.

Motivation distinguishes prompting without task-specific training from unseen-template generalization. No BERT baseline. slides.title: What makes one benchmark sample?
slides.script: Each sample combines a physical layout, a public instruction, a dependency graph, and a private preference. In this example, the robot must open a box, deliver the chosen item, and replace the lid. If the choice is missing, opening the box is still useful and already allowed. The robot only receives the instruction, visible state, and public interaction history. The true preference, evaluator verdict, and oracle trajectory stay private. This separation prevents either gate from reading the answer, or receiving a hidden label that tells it when to ask. The dependency graph makes task order explicit.
slides.evidence: data/three_task_v8/r2/test.jsonl; public serialization and private task specification. outputs/three_task_v8/report/summary.json; outputs/three_task_v8/frozen_manifest.json.

slides.title: Three tasks, three clarification regimes
slides.script: Our three task templates create different clarification situations. In buffer exchange, two occupied slots swap their contents through a temporary pad. If the user has not selected the permitted pad, the first move requires clarification. In retrieve and restore, the robot can open the box before asking which item to deliver. That tests whether a gate can delay a question until it blocks progress. In occlusion inspection, the missing information is a world fact. The robot must move the screen, inspect the label, and report the measured code. Asking the user would bypass a required observation. We also include fully disclosed controls. These structures distinguish asking first, making progress before asking, and inspecting instead of asking.
slides.evidence: data/three_task_v8/r2/{dev,test}.jsonl; public task DAGs. Inspection DAG: clear_screen, inspect_label, report_code; screen remains parked. Conceptual regimes are not a preregistered numerical timing metric.

slides.title: Build layouts first, then split by group
slides.script: We generate base layouts, assign groups, and separate Development from Test before adding preference or wording variants. Variants of one layout stay in the same partition. Development has twenty-four samples from six groups. Test has twelve samples from twelve independent groups, four per template. Both partitions balance zero and one unknown slot, and we balance the position of the correct choice in candidate order. Previously debugged layouts stay outside Test. A deterministic oracle then executes every sample with the real robot skills and independent evaluator. All thirty-six executions passed. These are feasibility checks across eighteen layouts, and the models never see the oracle actions.

slides.title: Three methods, one shared planner
slides.script: The comparison changes the gate while keeping planning shared. LLM-NoAsk skips the gate, never asks, and lets DeepSeek act from public information. It can guess an undisclosed preference. LLM-Gate uses DeepSeek to choose ASK or CONTINUE. Jev-Gate obtains a Noul probability and asks at the frozen threshold of zero point five. Jev returns typed probabilities instead of generating an answer token by token. That motivates lower decision overhead, but does not guarantee the right decision. Both gates see the same compact public state and run before planning. Every method uses the same DeepSeek action planner. Both asking methods share the question generator, simulator, physics and evaluator. Models, prompts and budgets were frozen before Test.

slides.title: Success, burden and inference overhead
slides.script: We measure three outcomes. Task success comes from the final physical world and required event order, not a DONE claim. The evaluator checks object footprints, support and stability, lid coverage where needed, and release from the robot. Clarification burden counts the distinct preference slots in each question. Repeated requests cost again. Inference overhead includes token usage by backend and measured API response time for every agent call, including DONE and retries. We also estimate dollars by applying each provider's current prices to its recorded usage, including DeepSeek cache hits. This is an API-only estimate, separate from robot runtime and human effort. Different backends' tokens are never treated as equivalent dollars.

slides.title: Reliability and whole-workflow latency
slides.script: We ran thirty-six real API and PyBullet episodes: twelve held-out layouts, each paired across three methods. NoAsk succeeded in ten cases. Both gates succeeded in twelve. NoAsk made two wrong guesses, one about the permitted buffer and one about the requested item. On the four cases with a genuinely undisclosed user preference, the outcomes were two out of four versus four out of four. That subset is very small. Both gates requested four slots in total, averaging one third per episode. NoAsk was fastest overall. Jev-Gate's cumulative API latency was about seventy-nine seconds, compared with one hundred and five for LLM-Gate, around twenty-five percent lower. These totals cover twelve episodes per method, not robot execution time.

slides.title: Gate speed and estimated API cost
slides.script: Looking only at gate calls, the average API response was eight hundred and fifteen milliseconds for DeepSeek and two hundred and ninety-five for Jev. That is about two point eight times faster in these saved runs. The calls follow different trajectories, so this is not a same-input speed benchmark. For dollars, we price actual cache hits, misses and outputs using public rates checked on November twelfth. The recorded DeepSeek requests fall in off-peak hours. Estimated total API costs across twelve episodes are roughly one point one cents for NoAsk, one point eight five cents for LLM-Gate, and one point seven eight cents for Jev-Gate. These are estimates, not invoices. Jev's whole-workflow saving is only about four percent. Shared planning still costs money, and DeepSeek caching is very cheap. The evidence supports reduced gate latency, with a modest estimated cost advantage in this configuration.

slides.title: Clarification timing changes the execution order
slides.script: Timing can differ even when success and burden match. On two retrieval cases with an unknown item, LLM-Gate asked before opening. Jev opened first, then asked. This is exploratory trace analysis. In the actual replay, Jev initially scores zero point eleven and the robot opens the box. The score then reaches zero point sixty-two. It asks which item to retrieve, and the simulator selects the block. Watch the robot deliver it and replace the lid. The replay also keeps a rejected generic lid move before the correct cover action repairs it. Recorded frames drive both robot motion and flow highlights together.

slides.title: Conclusions and next experiment
slides.script: Our contribution is an auditable benchmark for clarification timing. In this small study, both gates improved observed reliability over guessing. Jev reduced observed gate latency, while its estimated total cost saving was modest. We cannot claim general superiority or better zero-shot performance than BERT, which we did not test. Next, we will expand independent layouts, pre-register timing measures, and evaluate robustness and cost across repeated runs. Any tuning will use a new Development version, preserving this frozen Test result. Thank you.
